analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from collecting or selling people's reproductive and sexual health data without consent.
analysis.headline: A bill to keep period apps, advertisers, and data brokers from collecting or selling reproductive health information won support from 118 House Democrats but died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop most companies from collecting, keeping, or sharing personal reproductive or sexual health information — including pregnancy status, period and fertility data from apps, location data suggesting a clinic visit, and even data inferred by algorithms — unless the person gave written consent or the data was strictly needed to provide the requested service. It would give people the right to see and delete that data, force companies to publish privacy policies, and let the Federal Trade Commission and individuals sue violators, with invalid pre-dispute arbitration clauses. Doctors and hospitals already covered by HIPAA medical-privacy rules would be excluded.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose reproductive or sexual health data ends up in the hands of app makers, advertisers, or data brokers — most directly women who use period-tracking, fertility, or pregnancy apps, and people in states where abortion is restricted, since such data can reveal a pregnancy or a search for care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who use reproductive health apps and services

how_it_helps.text: Bars commercial entities from collecting, retaining, using, or disclosing personal reproductive or sexual health information without express written consent or unless strictly necessary to provide a requested product or service [S2][S3].
Covers inferred and location data — including information an algorithm derived, and location data that might indicate an attempt to obtain reproductive services [S3].
Gives individuals the right to access their data (including which third parties it was sold to) and a free mechanism to have it deleted within 15 days [S3].
Requires companies to publish a clear privacy policy listing which third parties they sell or share the data with [S3].

Provides enforcement by the Federal Trade Commission and private lawsuits with damages of at least $100 per violation per day, and voids pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers for these claims [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: App makers, advertisers, data brokers, and other companies that profit from collecting and monetizing reproductive and sexual health data would lose that revenue and face compliance costs, FTC penalties, and lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, adtech, and health app companies

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes doctors, hospitals, and other HIPAA-covered providers, so it protects app-based data but leaves the existing federal medical-privacy regime unchanged for clinical care [S2][S3].
The private right of action — at least $100 per violation per day plus fees — could invite voluminous or abusive litigation, a cost honest supporters of private enforcement generally acknowledge.
Compliance costs fall on businesses of every size, including small app developers and nonprofits, which must build consent, access, deletion, and published-policy systems or stop collecting the data.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: it closes a well-known gap in which fertility and period apps and the data-broker ecosystem collect and resell reproductive health information with almost no legal limit. The costs — compliance burdens and litigation risk — are real but bounded, and the strongest design critique is not the burden but the gap: by carving out HIPAA-covered entities, the bill protects data held by apps and brokers while leaving clinical records governed by a separate, older rule system. On balance it is a focused consumer-privacy bill rather than a sweeping one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023 without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sara Jacobs introduced the My Body, My Data Act of 2022 in the House on June 16, 2022, joined by 34 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and that was the last committee action of record [S5].
It eventually drew 117 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect, broker, and advertise against reproductive and sexual health data — period-trackers, adtech firms, and data brokers — keep operating without a federal consent or deletion requirement, and no one gained new privacy rights.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and app companies that monetize health data

for.name: Rep. Sara Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1][S5].

for.name: 117 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the largest bloc of support it received [S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 16, 2022 and took no further recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 117 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican support is recorded; the bill also never advanced far enough to force a recorded vote on the issue [S4][S5].

industries.note: These firms buy, infer, and resell reproductive health signals — including location data indicating clinic visits — and the bill would require consent and allow deletion, cutting off much of that trade [S3]. Their gain from the status quo comes directly from data people did not knowingly consent to sell.

industries.industry: Period-tracking, fertility, and pregnancy app makers
industries.note: The bill targets exactly the data these apps collect, forcing consent-based collection, published privacy policies, and deletion rights. Some already promised such practices voluntarily; the bill would make them enforceable.

industries.industry: HIPAA-covered health care providers and their business associates
industries.note: The bill expressly excludes entities covered by HIPAA medical-privacy rules, so clinics, hospitals, and insurers keep operating under the existing regime rather than a second one [S2][S3].
